claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys at high temperature is governed by optimization of configurational entropy.
Optimizing configurational entropy enhances resistance to thermal degradation.
Optimizing configurational entropy enhances resistance to phase separation.
The proposed initial materials are nanoalloys containing multiple principal elements in near-equal proportions.
Systematically varying alloy composition modifies configurational entropy.
The proposed test is conducted at temperatures above 500°C with controlled heating rates and exposure times.
Increased configurational entropy reduces the driving force for phase separation.
Increased configurational entropy promotes a more homogeneous microstructure.
Reduced phase-separation driving force and greater microstructural homogeneity enhance thermal stability.
Nanoalloys with optimized configurational entropy will show less phase separation than conventional low-configurational-entropy alloys.
Nanoalloys with optimized configurational entropy will show greater microstructural homogeneity than conventional low-configurational-entropy alloys.
Nanoalloys with optimized configurational entropy will show greater thermal resistance than conventional low-configurational-entropy alloys.
The comparison baseline consists of conventional alloys characterized as having low configurational entropy.
The prediction is restricted to the investigated temperature range of 500°C to 1000°C and to the investigated compositions.
The relationship between configurational entropy and thermal stability may depend on elemental identity and inter-element interactions.
